column2: The sound system: syllable, initials, simple finals and the four tones
Every syllable is made of an initial (声母) + a final (韵母) + a tone (声调). Example: mā = m + a + 1st tone.
b p m f · d t n l · g k h · j q x · zh ch sh r · z c s. Watch out for the unaspirated / aspirated pairs: b–p, d–t, g–k, j–q, zh–ch, z–c (the second one is pronounced with a puff of air).
a o e i u ü. ü is pronounced like the French “u” or the German “ü”: say “ee” while rounding your lips.
1st tone high and level (ˉ), 2nd rising (ˊ), 3rd low, dipping and rising (ˇ), 4th falling and sharp (ˋ). The mark is written above the main vowel. Changing the tone changes the meaning!
Mum rides a horse, the horse is slow, mum scolds the horse. (Great for the tones of “ma”!)
Compound finals (ai, ao…), nasal finals (-n / -ng), the final er and the retroflex 儿化
ai ei ao ou · ia ie ua uo üe · iao iou uai uei: glide from one vowel to the next without pausing.
an en in un ün end with the tongue against the teeth (n); ang eng ing ong with the back of the tongue (ng). Telling them apart is essential: fān ≠ fāng.
The final er and 儿化
er is pronounced by curling the tongue: 二 èr. Added to other syllables (儿化) it makes the final retroflex, typical of the north: 玩儿 wánr, 一点儿 yìdiǎnr.
Sorry, I don’t understand. Could you say it again, please?
The fertiliser evaporates. Black fertiliser turns grey, grey fertiliser turns black. (To tell f and h apart)
Pinyin (3): neutral tone, tone changes, spelling
Neutral tone, tone changes (3rd+3rd, 一, 不) and pinyin spelling rules
Some syllables are said short and light, without a tone: no mark is written. It often happens with the second repeated syllable (妈妈 māma, 谢谢 xièxie) and with particles such as 的, 了, 吗, 呢.
Two third tones in a row
When two 3rd tones meet, the first one is pronounced as a 2nd tone (but it is still written as a 3rd).
一 is read yī on its own or in numbers; before a 1st, 2nd or 3rd tone it becomes yì; before a 4th tone it becomes yí. Books often already write the changed tone.
不 is read bù, but before a 4th tone it becomes bú.

Without an initial: i → yi, u → wu, ü → yu. After j, q, x the ü is written u (ju, qu, xu); after l and n it keeps the dots (lü, nü). iou, uei, uen after an initial are shortened to iu, ui, un (niú, guì, lùn). In iu and ui the tone goes on the second vowel.
That’s too expensive! A bit less?
Wait a moment… eight yuan, OK?
A phoenix is painted on the pink wall. (For f / h and the nasals)
Greeting, introducing yourself, asking someone’s name and surname
A greeting you can use at any time of day. 您 is the polite form: use it with teachers and older people. You answer with the same greeting.
叫 + full name (or first name): “to be called”. 姓 + surname only: “to have the surname”. With older people you don’t ask 你叫什么名字, you ask their surname.
My name is Wang Ping, my surname is Wang.
Noun or pronoun + 呢 makes a short question that repeats the previous one.
都 goes after the subject (which must be plural) and before the verb.
A 的 B = “A’s B”. With close people (family, teachers, groups) 的 is often left out: 我们老师.
The first day, in front of the library
My name is Wang Ping, I’m Chinese. And you?
My name is Lisa, I’m an international student.
Hello everyone! My name is Yamada, I’m Japanese. I’m an international student. His name is Jeff, her name is Annie. We are all international students. Our teacher’s surname is Tian, she is Chinese.
Eight hundred soldiers run towards the northern slope, the gunners run side by side on the north side. (For b / p)
Morning greetings, asking nationality, age and class
Morning greeting (usually until 10 a.m.). You answer the same way. In the same way: 上午好、下午好、晚上好.
Statement + 吗 = yes/no question. To answer: 是 / 对 (yes), 不 + verb (no).
Are you American? — No, I’m French.
你多大 asks the age of people your age or younger. 几 asks for a small number (usually under 10): 几班? 几点? For age say number + 岁, without 是.
How old are you? — I’m twenty.
Which class are you in? — I’m in class 2.
也 always goes after the subject and before the verb: 我也是… You can’t say “也我”.
11 = 十一, 15 = 十五, 20 = 二十, 35 = 三十五, 99 = 九十九, 100 = 一百. Just combine tens (number + 十) and units.
I’m German. Which class are you in?
Class 2. Are you in class 2 too?
Annie is nineteen this year, she is American. Jeff is English and he is twenty. They are both in class 2. Peter is French, he is nineteen too, and he is in class 1.
Four is four, ten is ten, fourteen is fourteen, forty is forty. (For sì / shí)

In Chinese the surname comes before the given name: in 王平, Wang is the surname and Ping the given name. Almost all surnames have a single character (王, 李, 张, 刘, 陈…), a few have two (欧阳, 司马). Children are often given nicknames with a repeated character (明明) or with 小 in front (小王).
Telling the time, the days of the week, the class timetable
点 = o’clock, 分 = minutes, 半 = half, 刻 = quarter, 差 = to (minus). 8:00 八点 · 8:05 八点零五分 · 8:15 八点一刻 · 8:30 八点半 · 8:45 八点三刻 or 差一刻九点 · 8:55 差五分九点.
The days: 星期一 (Monday) … 星期六 (Saturday), 星期天 / 星期日 (Sunday). Before dates and days 是 can be left out.
What day is it today? — Today is Tuesday.
“from… to…”: for spans of time or space.
I have class from eight to ten.
For counting and in numbers use 二 (一、二、三; 十二; 二十). Before a measure word use 两: 两点, 两个人, 两天.
“It’s time to…”: 该 + verb + 了, according to the timetable or common sense.
It’s midnight, time to go to bed.
The negative of 有 is always 没有, never 不有.
I have no class this morning.
In the dorm, in the morning
Yes, at nine I have listening class.
Today is Tuesday. In the morning Lisa has spoken Chinese from 8:00 to 9:50 and Chinese characters from 10:00 to 11:50. In the afternoon she has no class. In the evening she goes to bed at 11:30.
Before my bed, the bright moonlight: it looks like frost on the ground. I raise my head and look at the moon, I lower my head and think of home.
Asking where a place is and giving directions, saying thank you; position (right, left, next to)
“Excuse me, may I ask…?”: put it at the start of a question to be polite.
Excuse me, where is the toilet?
To 谢谢 you reply 不用谢 or 不客气 (“you’re welcome”).
To say where something is: thing + 在 + reference point + (的) + 旁边/左边/右边/上边/下边. You say 宿舍的旁边, not 宿舍的旁.
The canteen is next to the dormitory.
这 = this (near), 那 = that (far), 哪 = which? With 儿 they indicate places: 这儿 (here), 那儿 (there), 哪儿 (where?). Before a measure word people often say zhèi, nèi, něi.
This is the classroom, that is the dormitory.
When the adjective is the predicate you don’t use 是, but usually 很: 学校很大 (not “学校是大”).
Excuse me, where is the international students’ dormitory?
It’s over there, to the left of the canteen.
To the right of this classroom.

Piao Zhiyong is in class 3. The class 3 classroom isn’t big, it’s to the right of the class 2 classroom. The international students’ canteen is very big, it’s next to the dormitory. The toilet is to the left of the classrooms.
Sleeping in spring I don’t notice the dawn; everywhere I hear birds singing. Last night, the sound of wind and rain: who knows how many flowers have fallen.
The monk carries soup up the pagoda; the pagoda is slippery, the soup spills and scalds the pagoda.
Shopping: prices, colours, measure words and completed actions
In speech people use 块 and 毛, in writing 元 and 角: 1 块 = 10 毛. A price is read unit by unit; the last unit can be dropped: ¥7.50 = 七块五 (毛); ¥15.40 = 十五块四; ¥2.05 = 两块零五分. Before 块 you say 两, not 二.
百 = hundred. 340 = 三百四十; 105 = 一百零五 (a zero in the middle is said 零); 200 = 二百 or, in speech, 两百.
Adjective / pronoun / place + 的 replaces a noun that is already clear from the context: 黑的 (the black one), 我的 (mine), 右边的 (the one on the right).
There are both black ones and blue ones.
I want the one on the right.
Between a number (or 这 / 那 / 哪) and a noun you need a measure word: 个 is general, 辆 for vehicles, 种 for kinds, 本 for books, 件 for clothes, 双 for pairs, 支 for pens, 杯 for glasses and cups.
two books, a cup of tea
了 after the verb shows that the action is completed; it is often followed by number + measure word + object. The negative is 没(有) + verb, without 了.
Asks for an opinion or makes a suggestion: “what about…?”.
What do you think of this colour?
What would you like to buy?
I’d like to buy some clothes.
I like blue. Do you have this one in blue?
We have it in blue and in white. What about the blue one?
Very nice. How much is it?
I’d also like a pair of shoes. How much is it altogether?

Today Jeff spent a lot of money. He bought three books, a pen and a white top. The books cost 30 yuan each, the pen 4.50 and the top 158 yuan. He also had a tea, 5 yuan. Today Jeff spent 257.50 yuan altogether.
Eat grapes without spitting out the skins; don’t eat grapes and yet spit out the skins.

In shops, canteens and even street stalls people almost always pay with their phone, by scanning a QR code. Cash is used less and less, but it’s good to be able to read prices: price tags say ¥ or 元, while in speech people say 块.
Making phone calls, phone and room numbers, dates, birthdays and invitations
Repeating the verb makes the action short and tentative, and the tone softer. One-syllable verbs: AA or A一A (看看 / 看一看); two-syllable verbs: ABAB (休息休息). The second verb has the neutral tone.
Have a look at this book.
They are read digit by digit. In phone and room numbers 1 is often said yāo, so it isn’t confused with 七 qī; 0 = 零 líng. For buildings: number + 号楼.
You answer or start a call with 喂 (often pronounced wéi). To ask who it is: 是…吗? / 你是谁? To answer: 是我 / 我是…
Hello, is that Wang Ping? — Speaking.
Sentence + 吧 = suggestion or invitation: “let’s…”, “come on…”.
给 introduces the person to whom (or for whom) the action is done; it goes before the verb.
I’d like to buy him a present.
Dates go from big to small: 月 + 号 (spoken) / 日 (written). For wishes: 祝 + person + wish.
When is your birthday? — On 9 October.
It’s Yamada. Are you free tomorrow evening?
Tomorrow is Annie’s birthday: let’s buy her a present together.
At six in the evening, at building 5. I live in 302.

Today is 12 October, Wang Ping’s birthday. Jeff, Annie and Yamada know. They bought Wang Ping a present: a Chinese book. At seven in the evening they go together to Wang Ping’s dormitory; he lives in building 3, room 506. Everyone says: “Happy birthday!” and Wang Ping answers: “Thank you all!”
Goose, goose, goose: with its curved neck it sings to the sky. White feathers float on the green water, red feet paddle the clear waves. (Written, they say, at the age of seven.)
On the table there is a basin, in the basin there is a bottle. (For -n / -ng with 儿化)
Feeling ill, asking for leave, apologising for being late
You ask this when someone seems unwell or something has happened: “what’s wrong?”, “what happened?”. To answer: body part + 疼.
What’s wrong? — I have a headache.
了 at the end of a sentence: change
了 at the end of a sentence signals a new situation: it wasn’t like this before, now it is.
Annie is ill, she can’t come to class today.
能 + verb: to be able to, or to have the possibility of doing something. Negative: 不能.
才 + verb: the action happens later or with more difficulty than expected. 你怎么才来? = “why are you only arriving now?”. With 才 you usually don’t use 了.
Why are you only getting here now?
I didn’t get up until half past eight.
请 + length of time + 假: 请一天假, 请半天假. To apologise: 对不起，我来晚了.
Ms Tian, I’d like to ask for a day off.
I had a cold, so I didn’t come to class.
I have a stomach ache, I can’t manage the class.
I don’t know. I’d like to ask for a day off and go back to my room to rest.
All right. Can you come tomorrow?

Today Peter didn’t get to class until nine. His alarm clock had stopped, so he didn’t get up until half past eight. Ms Tian asks him: “What happened?” Peter answers: “Sorry, I’m late.” Lisa didn’t come today either: she is ill and has a bad headache.
Two or three li along the way, a village in the mist with four or five houses; six or seven pavilions, eight, nine, ten flowers. (A rhyme for learning the numbers 1 to 10.)
Look at the sky: the sky full of stars; look at the ground: there’s a hole; look into the hole: there’s a plate of ice. (For -n / -ng)

In China the numbers 1 to 10 are shown with one hand: 6 = thumb and little finger out, 7 = fingertips pressed together, 8 = thumb and index finger in an “L”, 9 = index finger bent like a hook, 10 = closed fist or two crossed index fingers. On cheques and bank documents the “formal” numbers are used, which are hard to forge: 壹 贰 叁 肆 伍 陆 柒 捌 玖 拾.
Food and drink, tasting and bargaining at the market, offering something to a guest
“No problem”: a confident answer to a request or a doubt.
Can you finish it? — No problem!
Repeat the verb or adjective with 不 in between: 酸不酸? 是不是? 有没有? It is already a question: don’t add 吗.
可以 mostly expresses permission (“may I?”, “is it allowed?”); 能 an ability or a possibility. To ask for permission both work; to refuse it use 不能 or 不可以.
May I taste it? — Of course.
I can finish a jin of dumplings.
A unit of weight used at the market: 一斤 = 500 g, 半斤 = 250 g. You ask the price like this: 多少钱一斤?
